name: Robert Ackerman
title: Associate Professor
research_summary: Narcissism and the impact of individual differences on interpersonal relationships | Research Interests My research addresses questions about interpersonal relationships using methods and models from both social and personality psychology. It is characterized by three broad lines of work. First, I am interested in developmental factors that contribute to the functioning of adult romantic relationships. My second line of research focuses on how narcissistic attributes impact the development of relationships and how such attributes affect important relationship outcomes in ongoing relationships. Finally, because my substantive interests involve processes that occur within relationships and therefore often involve non-independent data, I am particularly interested in analytic models for both cross-sectional and longitudinal dyadic data.

name: Francesca Filbey
title: Bert Moore Chair in BrainHealth
research_summary: Addiction as a model to understand reward system dysfunction in humans using multimodal brain imaging techniques. | Research Interests: In the United States, addictive disorders including substance use disorders and pathological overeating cause an extensive burden in terms of morbidity, mortality, and public health costs, yet treatment strategies are only modestly effective.  Better understanding of the biological mechanisms that underlie addictive disorders and increase susceptibility could substantially improve current prevention and intervention efforts. The overarching goal across my line of translational research is to characterize factors that increase risk for addictive disorders. Specifically, I am interested in how early life factors such as period of exposure (e.g., adolescent onset of regular use) or early life stress mediate the neural mechanisms that are associated with addictive disorders, and how genetic risk moderates these effects.

name: Matthew Goeckner
title: Professor
research_summary: Physical Science Related Research the plasma state is still a wide open frontier, which we are struggling to understand and control. Plasmas are richly complex, encompassing an incredible diversity of linear and non-linear phenomena including atomic collisions, electromagnetic interactions, fluid dynamics, collective excitations, thermodynamics, chemical reactions, and radiation transport. This complexity presents a scientific and engineering challenge, but it also opens opportunities to achieve properties and performance that may not be achieved with other states of matter. Plus, many more c l The assumption that the electron energy distribution can be accurately described with a temperature is likely wrong. Specifically, the high-energy component of the energy distribution, which may or may not follow a Maxwellian distribution, often plays a major role in the collision processes at hand. Electron collision cross sections have not been determined for all of the important species, or some of them may have significant error. Many gas and surface-phase chemical reaction processes are unknown.
ai_review: Matthew Goeckner’s research within the Physics and Astronomy department centers on exploring the complexities of plasma physics, recognizing it as a largely uncharted scientific frontier. His work investigates the diverse phenomena within plasmas – including atomic collisions, electromagnetic interactions, and radiation transport – often utilizing computational fluid dynamics to model these intricate systems. A key focus is challenging traditional assumptions about electron energy distributions, specifically examining the significant role played by high-energy components that may deviate from Maxwellian statistics. Goeckner’s lab investigates these processes through detailed collision cross-section analysis, aiming to ultimately control and understand plasma behavior for potentially novel material properties.  Ultimately, his research seeks to overcome limitations in current understanding of plasma states and unlock new technological applications.

name: Roderick Heelis
title: Distinguished Chair in Natural Sciences and Mathematics Research Scientist
research_summary: Research Interests My primary research interests center around the analysis and interpretation of data from Earth orbiting satellites. These data describe the density and motion of charged particles in the upper atmosphere. Theses particles are strongly influenced by the Earth's magnetic field and by electric fields that arise from motions of the atmosphere and the interaction of the planet with the interplanetary medium. Our data sources from the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program and from FormosaSat-1 are very extensive and with data visualization tools we are constructing a global description of the dynamics of the charged particles and how it changes in response to variations on the Sun. In 2006 we will launch a new satellite-based experiment to examine the relationships between charged and neutral motions at low latitudes in the upper atmosphere. New instrumentation being flown in this mission will require extensive development of software to produce geophysical parameters that will make up a unique data set that has never before been available from space.

name: Christa McIntyre

research_summary:
Neural mechanisms of stress effects on memory and extinction of conditioned fear | Research Interests Information acquired during daily 
encounters is not readily encoded into memory, but requires some effort 
or rehearsal to be preserved. In contrast, experiences that are either 
arousing or emotionally meaningful in content appear to be permanently 
stored into memory without conscious effort. My research is aimed at 
understanding the effect of emotional arousal on memory storage. 
Research findings to date indicate that events that are sufficiently 
arousing to be remembered for the long-term lead to activation of the 
amygdala. This amygdala activation may, in turn, initiate long-term 
memory storage by influencing synaptic strength in other areas of the 
brain, such as the hippocampus and cortex. I am currently using in vivo 
microdialysis, western blots, immunohistochemstry and in situ 
hybridization to better understand how emotion-induced amygdala activity
 may modulate the expression of synaptic proteins in areas that underlie
 memory storage.

research_summary: Molecular characterization of human pain-sensing neurons; chronic pain mechanisms; development of novel pain therapeutics | Research Interests Pain Research in the Price Lab Pain Research in the Price Lab Pain serves a vital teaching function because it instructs organisms to avoid harmful stimuli. Pain plasticity is likewise a key feature of complex nervous systems because it signals for an organism to protect an injured area until the healing process has run its course. While these pain amplification mechanisms frequently resolve following healing, they can persist manifesting as chronic pain conditions. Moreover, chronic pain conditions (e.g. migraine headache) can arise without any apparent precipitating stimulus. Unfortunately these chronic pain conditions are poorly treated by current therapies creating an enormous burden of suffering with an economic impact estimated to be greater than diabetes, heart disease and cancer, combined! Hence, there is a great need to better understand mechanisms driving chronic pain and tailored therapeutic approaches that can reverse this aberrant plasticity.

name: Lucien Thompson
title: Emeritus Associate Professor
research_summary: Aging, with an emphasis on learning and memory, neuronal excitability, loss and recovery of function, and nootropic (memory-enhancing) drugs | Research Interests As a cellular- and systems-level neuroscientist, I strive to understand and improve the basic cellular mechanisms of learning and memory. I have concentrated my research efforts on regulation of post-synaptic excitability, more specifically, the necessary role of Ca2+-dependent K+ channels. These K+ channels play a crucial role in memory-related plasticity across the lifespan. They interact strongly with NMDA (NR) excitatory glutamate receptors to regulate excitability in Hebbian models, and bridge important gaps in multiple forms of meta-plasticity critical for memory consolidation. Our work shows that plasticity of these K+ channels is highly conserved: across different species, different tasks, and across brain regions (i.e. they are a necessary convergence point in learning and in memory consolidation).
ai_review: Lucien Thompson’s research within the Psychological Brain Sciences department investigates the cellular mechanisms underlying aging and its impact on learning and memory. Focusing specifically on neuronal excitability, Dr. Thompson's lab explores the role of calcium-dependent potassium channels in regulating synaptic plasticity – particularly through their interaction with NMDA receptors – a process central to Hebbian models and memory consolidation. His work centers on understanding how these K+ channel dynamics contribute to both age-related cognitive decline and potential recovery of function, ultimately seeking to identify targets for nootropic interventions. Notably, Thompson’s research demonstrates the conservation of this K+ channel plasticity across diverse species, tasks, and brain regions, suggesting a critical convergence point in learning and memory processes. Through detailed investigations at the cellular and systems level, Dr. Thompson aims to bridge gaps in our understanding of meta-plasticity and its implications for cognitive health throughout life.

ai_review: Michael Zhang, currently a professor in bioengineering at the University of Texas at Dallas, conducts research focused on integrating genomic and proteomic data to understand complex biological regulatory networks. His background includes a strong engineering foundation from USTC combined with expertise in statistical physics gained during his doctoral studies at Rutgers University, followed by postdoctoral work in applied mathematics. His recent publications demonstrate an interest in translating large datasets into actionable insights regarding cancer biology.

Her work investigates the persistence of carbon in Earth systems by examining reactions occurring at these interfaces, often focusing on coastal wetland soils and atmospheric nanoparticle deposition. Zhao’s research employs a combination of experimental approaches, including investigations into greenhouse gas production influenced by salinity and soil characteristics, alongside advanced analytical techniques like aerosol mass spectrometry to quantify nanoplastic particle composition and loading. Ultimately, Professor Zhao’s lab seeks mechanistic insights into carbon dynamics with significant implications for broader Earth system science.

ai_review: Yujie Zheng’s research within the Physics and Astronomy department centers on utilizing radar remote sensing techniques, primarily InSAR, to investigate critical hydrological processes and tectonic activity. Her work focuses heavily on extracting quantitative information from satellite-based radar data, employing methods like closure phase analysis and spatiotemporal velocity mapping to model and predict surface soil moisture and near-surface seismic velocities. ai_review: Hejun Zhu’s research within the geosciences department focuses on utilizing seismological techniques to investigate subsurface deformation and monitor environmental changes. His work primarily employs full-waveform inversion, ambient seismic noise monitoring, and spectral-element simulations to study processes occurring in the middle and lower crust, notably examining differential vertical motion along the Ordos Block. Specifically, Zhu investigates earthquake dynamics and utilizes seismic data to track baseflow and groundwater variations in sensitive environments like Yellowstone National Park and Central Oklahoma. Furthermore, he is developing advanced computational methods, including truncated pseudo-differential operators, for viscoacoustic reverse-time migration, aiming to refine understanding of wave propagation within viscoelastic media.
